readingInstruction: Read Psalm 52 and Psalm 53. The first is a psalm about a powerful, boastful man who is destroyed. The second is a near twin of Psalm 14, with the fool who says there is no God. Notice the contrast with the green olive tree.
settingTheScene: Psalm 52 has the title “when Doeg the Edomite, came and told Saul, David has come to the house of Ahimelech.” You read that story in Unit 9 (1 Samuel 22). Psalm 53 is a variation of Psalm 14, which you read earlier. Both psalms are by David, and they deal with the arrogance of evil and the fate of those who reject God. Together they fit a unit about a nation that forgot God.
observation: “Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day” (52:1).
“Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit” (52:2).
“You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right” (52:3).
“But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent” (52:5).
“See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches” (52:7).
“But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever” (52:8).
“The fool says in his heart, There is no God” (53:1).
“Oh that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad” (53:6).
interpretation:
Psalm 52 addresses Doeg directly, a man who used his power and his tongue to destroy the priests of Nob. David asks the question that exposes all boasting in evil: “Why do you boast?” The wicked man has power, but he does not have God’s steadfast love, which “endures all the day.” Evil has a limited life. The psalm describes a tongue like a razor, a man who loves lies, a man who trusts in riches. And it declares that God will break him down.

The central image is the contrast. The wicked man will be uprooted from his tent and from the land of the living. David, by contrast, is “like a green olive tree in the house of God.” An olive tree is long-lived and fruitful. It is planted in God’s house, in the place of his presence. The wicked man is torn out. The righteous man is rooted. The difference lies in where each puts his trust: in riches, or in “the steadfast love of God forever and ever.”

The psalm ends with thanksgiving. David says he will thank God forever for what he has done, and “wait for your name, for it is good.” He does not take revenge. He waits.

Psalm 53 is almost the same as Psalm 14, with small changes, and the repetition makes a point. The human heart’s tendency to say, “There is no God,” is not an occasional problem. It is universal. “They have all fallen away; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.” The Psalter wants us to hear this twice, so that we do not forget how deep the problem is.

Verse 5 adds a unique line: “There they were in great terror, where there was no terror, for God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you.” God defeats those who oppose his people, sometimes by simply causing fear. And again the psalm ends with the prayer for salvation to come out of Zion.
connection: Jesus is the root and the vine in whom we are planted (John 15:5). Psalm 1 and Jeremiah 17:7-8 echo the image of the tree. Paul quotes Psalm 14 and 53 in Romans 3:10-12 to prove that all are sinners, and he points to Christ as the answer (Romans 3:21-26). 1 Timothy 6:17 warns the rich not to trust in uncertain riches. Salvation did come out of Zion in Jesus (Romans 11:26).
application:
Name something you boast in. Bring it to God and ask for humility.

Thank God that you are planted in his house like an olive tree.

Pray, “Oh that salvation would come out of Zion,” for someone who does not yet know Christ.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from boasting in evil or trusting in riches.
Ask him to plant you like an olive tree in his house.
Confess where you have lived as though there is no God.
